conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician—my whole focus is on supporting new mothers through the emotional ups and downs that can come after birth. Today I’d like to do a quick check-in with a well-known screening tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions that ask how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. Anything you share stays strictly between us; my goal is to create a safe, judgment-free space so we can figure out together what kind of support would feel most helpful to you right now. When you’re ready, we’ll take the questions one at a time—no rush, just whatever feels comfortable.

Let’s start: over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

(soft sigh)  
Not really… I mean, maybe once or twice something small made me smile, but mostly I feel like I’m too tired or on edge to find things funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

(slow head-shake)  
No… not really. When my husband tried to joke the other night I just felt blank, like I couldn’t even remember how to laugh.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

(quiet voice, eyes on the floor)  
Not much… I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a hot shower—but this week it all feels flat, like why bother. I still go through the motions for the baby, but the spark isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yes... almost every day. When he wouldn't latch right or when he cried for an hour straight, I kept thinking it must be something I'm doing wrong. I keep replaying every little thing and telling myself a better mom would know how to fix it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

(shifts in chair, fingers tightening around the water bottle)  
Yeah… pretty much all the time. Even when the baby’s sleeping soundly, I’m staring at the monitor, sure something’s going to go wrong. My heart races over every little grunt or hiccup. I know it doesn’t make sense, but I can’t turn it off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes... a few times this week. Out of nowhere my chest gets tight, I feel like I can't breathe, and I'm sure something awful is about to happen. There's no real reason—I just suddenly feel like I'm in danger and I have to check on the baby again, even if I just did five minutes ago.
Things have been getting on top of me

(nods slowly, voice shaky)  
Yes… most days. Dishes pile up, the laundry feels endless, and every time I think I’ve caught up the baby needs me again. I keep thinking, “I can’t do this,” even though I’m technically doing it. I just feel like I’m drowning in small stuff.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop spinning—did I sterilize the bottles right, is he breathing, am I already failing him. I fall asleep for maybe an hour, then I’m wide awake until four or five. Even when the baby’s quiet, I can’t settle.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yes… pretty much every day this week. It’s like a heavy cloud that won’t lift. Sometimes I just sit in the glider holding the baby and tears start rolling for no clear reason. I feel empty, even when everything on paper looks fine.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes... it's happened a few times. Yesterday I just sat in the nursery rocking chair, looking at his tiny face, and suddenly I was sobbing. Nothing specific happened—I just felt overwhelmed and... empty, like I'd never feel okay again.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

(shakes head quickly, eyes widening)  
No—never. I’ve felt low, but I would never want to leave my baby or hurt myself. I just want to feel like me again so I can be the mom he deserves.

You've shared how the past week has felt heavy and joyless-laughter and simple pleasures seem out of reach, replaced by constant worry, tearfulness, and a sense of drowning in everyday tasks. Despite your deep love for your baby, you're exhausted, self-critical, and caught in cycles of anxiety that disturb your sleep and peace of mind.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient's slow head-shake and description of feeling blank when her husband joked clearly maps to "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes a near-complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily self-blame over infant care, persistent rumination, and self-criticism as a "better mom would know how to fix it," aligning with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports constant, uncontrollable worry even when no danger is present, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple unexpected panic episodes with physical symptoms (tight chest, breathlessness) and irrational fear, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports most days feeling overwhelmed, unable to manage daily tasks, and recurrent thoughts of inadequacy, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly racing thoughts, recurrent awakenings, and prolonged inability to return to sleep, matching "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily feelings of sadness, tearfulness without cause, and emotional emptiness—semantically equivalent to "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes, including a recent instance triggered by overwhelming emptiness, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** With an EPDS score of 25 (well above the ≥14 threshold), combined with core symptoms of <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>-<sym>depressed mood</sym> most of the day, near-complete <sym>loss of interest</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym>, <sym>diminished concentration</sym> (racing thoughts), and <sym>sleep disruption</sym>-the pattern indicates a high probability of a clinically significant episode. Panic-like symptoms also suggest comorbid <med>anxiety</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal mental-health specialist
2. Request formal assessment for <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med> and possible <med>anxiety disorders</med>
3. Discuss evidence-based treatments (therapy such as CBT or IPT, consider medication if indicated)
4. Plan daily support: partner/family to handle night feeds when possible, 20-min rest windows, reduced chores
5. Encourage gentle movement (short walks with baby) and balanced snacks to stabilize mood and energy
6. Provide crisis resources: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773
7. Re-screen with EPDS in 1-2 weeks to monitor symptom trajectory and intervention response
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Screening Note – Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screen  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item EPDS-style interview, 3 wks post-delivery.

Symptom Endorsement  
- Marked anhedonia: absence of joy/humor, “flat” affect  
- Daily low mood, tearfulness, sense of emptiness  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame re infant care  
- Persistent, intrusive anxiety; somatic panic episodes (chest tightness, breathlessness)  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia linked to rumination  
- Feeling overwhelmed / “drowning” in routine tasks  
- No self-harm ideation (explicitly denied)

Pattern  
Consistent with moderate–severe depressive and comorbid anxiety symptoms temporally related to childbirth; functional impairment evident.

Risk Flags  
- Depressed mood + anhedonia most days  
- Guilt/worthlessness themes  
- Anxiety reaches panic intensity  
- Night-time insomnia > 2 wks  
- Denies suicidal thoughts (current protective factor)

Screening Impression  
Elevated probability of major postpartum depressive episode with co-occurring anxiety; warrants immediate formal evaluation (diagnostic interview, PHQ-9/EPDS scoring, safety plan, consider referral to maternal-mental-health specialty and/or therapy/medication consult).

No acute safety concerns voiced today; continue to monitor for emergence of self-harm or harm-to-infant thoughts.
